content: Patients with diabetes mellitus have diverse educational needs, including guidance on diet, blood glucose monitoring, and treatment regimens. In many healthcare systems, specialist nurses play a pivotal role in addressing these needs, with the primary goal of empowering patients to manage their diabetes independently. This review was conducted to evaluate the impact of specialist nurse involvement on clinical outcomes for individuals with diabetes, compared to standard care provided in hospital clinics or primary care settings without specialist nurse input. The objective of this review was to determine the effects of diabetes specialist nurses or nurse case managers on the metabolic control of patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus. To achieve this, a thorough search of databases such as the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, and EMBASE was performed to identify relevant trials. Additionally, bibliographies of pertinent studies were reviewed, and manual searches of related publications were conducted to ensure comprehensive coverage. The review included randomized controlled trials and controlled clinical trials that examined the impact of specialist nurse practitioners on both short-term and long-term outcomes in diabetes management. Data extraction and quality assessment were independently conducted by three investigators, with any disagreements resolved through consensus. A total of six trials involving 1,382 participants, with follow-up periods ranging from six to twelve months, were included in the review. Two of these trials focused on adolescent populations. Due to significant variability among the trials, a meta-analysis was not feasible. The findings revealed that glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels in the intervention groups were not significantly different from those in the control groups over a 12-month follow-up period. However, one study reported a significant reduction in HbA1c levels at six months when a diabetes specialist nurse or nurse case manager was involved. One trial identified notable differences in the frequency of hypoglycemic and hyperglycemic episodes between the intervention and control groups. However, where reported, there were no significant differences in emergency hospital admissions or quality of life between the groups. The review did not provide information on body mass index (BMI), mortality rates, long-term diabetic complications, adverse effects, or healthcare costs. In conclusion, the involvement of a diabetes specialist nurse or nurse case manager may lead to improved glycemic control over short periods. However, the evidence from currently available trials does not demonstrate sustained benefits over longer durations. Additionally, there were no significant overall differences in the occurrence of hypoglycemic or hyperglycemic episodes, hospital admissions, or quality of life outcomes associated with specialist nurse care.
